title: British explanation: law’s rigor vs gospel fatherly dealing with infirmities
source_text: XII. Cui Thesi hanc statim subjungunt declarationem & confirmationem. Ex legis quidem rigore quodvis, vel levissimum peccatum est mortiferum, & excludit peccatorem a favore Dei, & regno coelorum. Sed cum filiis cum Christo jam adoptatis Deus non agit semper secundum legis rigorem. Sunt quidem peccata aliqua in quae si filii Dei incidant, & in quibus si perseverent, Deus eos ira sua prosequitur, & a regno coelorum excludendos denuntiat. 1 Cor. 6. 10. Gal. 5. 21. Coloss. 3. 6. de quibus in Thesibus sequentibus dicetur. Sunt autem & alia quaedam peccata, ob quae Deus misericors non solet filios suos, vel ad tempus, lumine vultus sui privare, nec metum condemnationis, aut mortis illis incutere. Hujusmodi sunt subiti & indeliberati rebellis concupiscentiae motus, de quibus conqueritur Apostolus Rom. 7. Item defectus & naevi, qui etiam optimis renatorum operibus adhaerescunt. Denique ea quotidiana humanae infirmitatis delicta, quae committuntur absque certo aliquo proposito ea committendi, & quotidiana remissionis postulatione dimittuntur. De hisce Jacobus 3. 2. In multis offendimus omnes; 1 Joh. 1. 8. Si dixerimus quoniam peccatum non habemus, ipsi nos seducimus. Hisce peccatis non obstantibus recte dixerit quivis fidelium, Nihil condemnationis est iis qui sunt in Christo Jesu. Imo in medio harum calamitatum, cuivis justificato Deus dicit quod Apostolo dixit, Sufficit tibi gratia mea; nam virtus mea in infirmitate perficitur. Non excidunt a statu justificationis suis infirmitatibus, quarum infirmitate virtus Dei perficitur, quique interim gloriari possint virtute Christi in se habitare, ut eodem loco habetur.
pass_a_gloss: To which Thesis they at once subjoin this declaration and confirmation. By the rigor of the law indeed any sin, even the lightest, is death-bringing, and excludes the sinner from God’s favor and the kingdom of heaven. But with sons already adopted with Christ God does not always deal according to the rigor of the law. There are indeed some sins into which if the sons of God fall, and in which if they persevere, God pursues them with his wrath and denounces them as to be excluded from the kingdom of heaven—of which it will be spoken in the following Theses. But there are also certain other sins on account of which merciful God is not wont to deprive his sons, even for a time, of the light of his countenance, nor to strike into them the fear of condemnation or of death. Of this kind are the sudden and indeliberate motions of rebellious concupiscence of which the Apostle complains in Romans 7; also the defects and blemishes which cling even to the best works of the regenerate; finally those daily faults of human infirmity which are committed without any certain purpose of committing them, and are dismissed by the daily asking of remission. Of these James 3:2, In many things we all offend; 1 John 1:8. These sins not hindering, any of the faithful may rightly say, There is no condemnation to them that are in Christ Jesus. Nay in the midst of these calamities God says to any justified person what he said to the Apostle, My grace is sufficient for thee; for my strength is made perfect in weakness. They do not fall from the state of justification by their infirmities, by whose weakness the power of God is perfected, and who meanwhile may glory that the power of Christ dwells in them, as is had in the same place.
pass_b_english: Law’s rigor makes every sin deadly; yet God does not always so deal with adopted sons.
Sudden lust-motions, flaws in best works, and unplanned daily slips leave no condemnation in Christ—and do not cast off justification.
